t.2.85.51: Women with lovely eyes came hurrying up to massage them, and after duly rubbing them down, those excellent women gave them drink.
t.2.85.52: The mighty attendants fed the mounts of the foremost Ikṣvāku warriors, the horses, elephants, donkeys, camels and likewise the sons of Surabhi, with sugarcane and honeycombs, urging them to eat.
t.2.85.53: The horse-keeper did not recognize his horse, nor the elephant-handler his elephant; that army, drunken, heedless and joyful, shone forth there.
t.2.85.54: Sated with every object of desire, smeared with red sandalwood paste, and joined by troops of apsarases, those soldiers raised their voices and spoke these words.
t.2.85.55: We shall not go to Ayodhyā, nor would we go to the Daṇḍakas. May Bharata have well-being, and may Rāma likewise have happiness.
t.2.85.57: Overjoyed, those men, the followers of Bharata, shouted there by the thousands, and they said, "This is heaven!"
t.2.85.59: Servants, maidservants and young wives, and the soldiers of the army too, all without exception, became thoroughly satisfied, and all of them were clad in new, unworn garments.
t.2.85.58: Then, though they had already eaten that food which was like nectar, on beholding those divine delicacies their minds turned once more to eating.
t.2.85.61: There was no one there in soiled clothes, nor hungry, nor dirty; not a single man was seen whose hair was dishevelled with dust.
t.2.85.60: Elephants, donkeys and camels, cattle and horses, beasts and birds were all well fed there, for no one had to provide for another.
t.2.85.62: With dishes of goat and of boar, with heaps of the choicest sauces, and with soups well prepared from fruit juices, rich in fragrance and flavour.
t.2.85.64: Along the edges of the forest there appeared wells whose mire was milk-rice, and those cows became wish-yielding, and the trees dripped with honey.
t.2.85.63: All around, the astonished men saw there thousands of iron vessels adorned with flowers and banners and filled with white rice.
t.2.85.65: There were ponds filled with maireya liquor, surrounded by heaps of savory meat, and by heated cauldrons as well, with the flesh of deer, peacocks and fowl.
t.2.85.66: There were thousands of golden vessels, and plates, pots and pans, well prepared and filled with curd, curd of the young, yellow and fragrant wood-apple.
t.2.85.67: There were ponds filled with rasāla, and others with white curds, and beside the milk-rice lay heaps of sugar.
t.2.85.68: At the bathing places of the rivers the men saw cleansing pastes, powders and astringent lotions, and many kinds of bathing preparations set out in vessels.
t.2.85.70: There, by the thousands, were polished mirrors, heaps of garments, and pairs of sandals and shoes.
t.2.85.69: They also saw heaps of white, gleaming tooth-cleaning sticks, and white sandal paste kept in caskets.
t.2.85.71: Caskets of collyrium, combs and brushes, parasols and bows, bright coats of mail guarding the vital parts, and beds and seats as well.
t.2.85.73: And there on every side they saw heaps of soft fodder, colored like dark blue beryl, laid out for feeding the animals.
t.2.85.72: Having plunged into the brimming watering-pools of the donkeys, camels, elephants and horses, and into lakes with fine bathing-places, full of blue water-lilies and lotuses,
t.2.85.74: Those men were filled with amazement on seeing that dreamlike marvel, such hospitality shown to Bharata by the great sage.
t.2.85.75: Thus, as they took their delight in the lovely hermitage of Bharadvāja like the gods in the Nandana garden, that night passed away.
t.2.85.76: Taking leave of Bharadvāja, those rivers, the gandharvas, and all those beautiful women returned the way they had come.
t.2.85.77: Just so, the men remained intoxicated, overpowered by wine; just so, they were still sprinkled with heavenly aloe and sandal paste; and just so lay the many kinds of heavenly, excellent garlands, scattered here and there and trampled by the people.
t.2.85.56: Thus the foot soldiers, and the riders and grooms of the elephants and horses, having received that lavish hospitality and finding themselves without masters, gave voice to these words.
t.2.85.2: But Bharata said to him, "Surely you have already done this: water for the feet, the guest-offering, and such hospitality as is possible in the forest."
t.2.85.1: Then the sage invited Bharata, the son of Kaikayī, who had resolved to stay there, to partake of his hospitality.
t.2.85.3: Then Bharadvāja, as if smiling, said to Bharata: "I know that you are full of affection, and that you would be satisfied with anything whatsoever."
t.2.85.4: I wish to provide food for this army of yours. My affection for you is fitting, and you are worthy of it, O bull among men.
t.2.85.5: And for what reason have you come here, having left your army far away? Why have you not come here together with your army, O bull among men?
t.2.85.6: With joined palms, Bharata replied thus to that ascetic rich in penance: "O blessed one, I have not come here with my army, out of fear of your holiness."
t.2.85.7: O blessed one, the finest horses, men, and choice elephants in rut follow me, covering a vast expanse of ground.
t.2.85.8: So that they might not harm the trees, the water, the ground, and the huts in the hermitages, I have therefore come here alone.
t.2.85.9: "Let the army be brought here," so was Bharata commanded by the supreme seer; and Bharata did accordingly, bringing about the approach of the army.
t.2.85.10: Then, entering the fire-sanctuary, he sipped water and wiped his lips, and for the sake of performing hospitality he summoned Viśvakarman.
t.2.85.11: I summon Viśvakarman and Tvaṣṭṛ as well. I wish to offer hospitality; let arrangements be made for me in that matter.
t.2.85.12: Let all the rivers that flow eastward and those that flow westward, on the earth and in the sky, assemble here today from every side.
t.2.85.14: I summon the gods and the Gandharvas, Viśvāvasu, Hahā and Huhū, and likewise the divine Apsarases and the Gandharva women, all of them together.
t.2.85.13: Let some rivers flow with maireya, others with well-prepared surā, and still others with cool water like the juice of sugarcane stalks.
t.2.85.15: Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, Miśrakeśī and Alambusā, and the lovely women who wait upon Śakra and those who wait upon Brahmā, all of them I summon, together with Tumburu and with their retinues.
t.2.85.17: Here may the blessed Soma provide for me excellent food, abundant and of many kinds: food to be chewed, food to be eaten, food to be sucked, and food to be licked.
t.2.85.16: The divine forest that lies among the Kurus, whose leaves are garments and ornaments and whose fruits are ever heavenly women, that very forest of Kubera appeared right here.
t.2.85.18: Colorful garlands and flowers fallen from the trees, drinks such as surā, and meats of many kinds as well.
t.2.85.19: Thus spoke the sage, absorbed in meditative concentration and endowed with incomparable splendour and austerity, uttering words perfect in articulation and accent.
t.2.85.20: As he meditated with his mind, facing east with joined palms, all those deities came, each one separately.
t.2.85.21: Then a breeze that dispelled sweat, having touched Malaya and Dardura, blew in due measure, delightful in its very nature, pleasant and auspicious.
t.2.85.23: Excellent breezes blew, and troops of Apsarases danced; the divine Gandharvas sang, and the vīṇās gave forth their notes.
t.2.85.22: Then heavenly clouds and showers of flowers came forth, and the sound of the gods' kettledrums was heard in all directions.
t.2.85.24: That sound, uttered smooth and even and endowed with the qualities of rhythm, entered the heavens and the earth and the ears of living beings.
t.2.85.26: For the ground on every side, for five yojanas around, became level, covered with abundant grassy meadows that shone like dark blue vaiḍūrya gems.
t.2.85.25: When that divine sound, delightful to the ears of men, had ceased, the army of Bharata beheld the arrangements made by Viśvakarman.
t.2.85.27: In that place there sprang up bael trees and wood-apples, jackfruits and citrons, emblic myrobalans and mangoes, all adorned with fruit.
t.2.85.28: From the Northern Kurus came a forest rich in divine delights, and there came also a divine river, lined with many trees growing along its banks.
t.2.85.30: And the royal palace too, resembling a white cloud, with its fine arched gateways, its form adorned with white garlands, was sprinkled all over with heavenly fragrances.
t.2.85.29: There were gleaming four-halled courtyard houses and stables for elephants and horses, clusters of mansions and palaces, and splendid archways.
t.2.85.31: It was four-sided and spacious, furnished with beds, seats and carriages, endowed with all heavenly flavours, and stocked with celestial food and garments.
t.2.85.32: It was a splendid place, where every kind of food had been prepared and the vessels were washed clean and spotless, where seats of every kind were set out and the finest beds were well spread.
t.2.85.33: Permitted by the great sage, the mighty-armed Bharata, son of Kaikayī, entered that dwelling filled with jewels.
t.2.85.34: All the ministers, together with the family priests, followed him, and seeing that arrangement of dwellings, they were filled with joy.
t.2.85.35: There stood a divine royal throne, a fan and a parasol; Bharata, together with his ministers, reverently circled them as though they were the king himself.
t.2.85.36: Bowing low to Rāma, he paid homage to the seat, and taking up a yak-tail fan, he sat down on the minister's seat.
t.2.85.37: All the ministers and family priests sat down in due order; then, after them, the commander of the army and the chief administrator sat down.
t.2.85.38: Then and there, within a moment, by the command of Bharadvāja, rivers whose mud was milk-rice came to wait upon Bharata.
t.2.85.40: And at that very moment there came twenty thousand women, adorned with divine ornaments, sent by Brahmā.
t.2.85.39: On both banks of those rivers stood delightful, divine dwellings plastered with white clay, brought into being by the grace of Brahmā.
t.2.85.41: Twenty thousand women sent by Kubera came, adorned with gold, gems and pearls, and with coral.
t.2.85.42: From Nandana came twenty thousand troops of Apsarases, by whom a man, once seized, is seen to be as if maddened.
t.2.85.43: Nārada, Tumburu, Gopa, Parvata and Sūryavarcasa, these kings of the Gandharvas, sang before Bharata.
t.2.85.44: Alambusā, Miśrakeśī, Puṇḍarīkā and Vāmanā danced before Bharata at the command of Bharadvāja.
t.2.85.45: The garlands that are found among the gods, and those that are found in the Caitraratha forest, were seen at Prayāga by the command of Bharadvāja.
t.2.85.46: By the power of Bharadvāja, the bilva trees became drummers, the vibhītaka trees became time-keepers beating the clappers, and the aśvattha trees became dancers.
t.2.85.47: Then the sarala and tāla trees, the tilakas and the naktamālas, full of delight, assembled there, having become hunchbacks and dwarfs.
t.2.85.48: The śiṃśapā, the āmalakī and the jambū trees, and the other creepers that were in the forest, took on the form of young women and dwelt in Bharadvāja's hermitage.
t.2.85.49: O drinkers of surā, drink surā; you who are hungry, drink pāyasa; and let the choicest meats be eaten as much as you desire.
t.2.85.50: On the lovely riverbanks, seven or eight young women at a time massaged each man with fragrant unguents and then bathed him.
